newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Rio state wants to change Banerj sale rules.
newsitem.headline: Rio state wants to change Banerj sale rules.

text.p: Rio de Janeiro state government has proposed changing the rules for privatizing its bank Banerj in an effort to draw more investors, said Rio Planning Secretary Marco Aurelio Alencar.

Under the proposal presented to Brazil's Central Bank, pension funds, non-financial companies and Banerj employees would be allowed to form consortia to buy control of Banerj as long as the groups are led by a financial institution, he said.
Previously, only banks were allowed to participate in the auction.
The Rio Planning Secretary also said the financial institution which will lead a group of bidders will be required to have a minimum 20 percent stake in the consortium.
He also said the bank must retain its stake in Banerj for at least five years and will be only allowed to sell its shares to another financial institution authorized by the Central Bank.
Rio de Janeiro state has also suggested that the privatization could be a 50 percent purchase of Banerj's capital plus one share, instead of the acquisition of 100 percent of the bank.
"We are reviewing the whole process in order to attract more investors. We are discussing all possibilities," Alencar said.
He also said that the bank's 480 million real base price and the amount of privatization bonds that investors will be allowed to use in the auction could also be reviewed.
Banerj's sale was postponed twice late last year due to court rulings against the bank's privatization.
But weak investor interest has also been an obstacle to privatization, analysts say.
At the time Banerj was put on sale, only two of eight pre-qualified bidders, private banks Bradesco and Banco Itau, signed up to participate in the auction.
After two failed attempts, the state decided to revise the rules to make it easier to privatize.
Although no date has been set for the publication of Banerj's new bid specifications and sell-off, Alencar said he hopes to put the bank on the block in May.
In addition to new privatization rules, Banerj's sell-off hinges on Senate approval of a deal which calls for the rescheduling of most of Rio de Janeiro state's debt, including that owed to Banerj.
The agreement, signed by state and federal officials earlier this year, also allows the federal government to lend the state some 2.9 billion reais to facilitate Banerj's privatization.
